summary: Extends the Sieve email filtering language so scripts can examine and change the MIME parts of a message. It adds ways to test parts, loop over them, extract text, and replace or enclose parts. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
Sieve is the language a mail server uses to write filtering rules, such as moving a message into a folder or deleting it. The base language can only look at the top of a message, and it has no way of repeating an action over several things.

This document lets a script walk through every part of a message, one part at a time, and act on each of them. It also lets the script read the headers inside a part rather than only the ones at the top, replace a part with different text, wrap the whole message in a warning, and copy text out of a part into a variable.

questions: how to filter mime parts with sieve
how does the sieve replace action work
subtitle: Lets a Sieve filtering script look inside a MIME message, walk its parts, and change or wrap what they find.

tldr.problem: MIME messages are often complex objects with many parts and sub-parts, and the base Sieve language has no way to look inside them. It also has no loop, so a filter cannot apply the same rule to every part of a message.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds a foreverypart loop that walks every MIME part depth first, a break command to leave it early, and :mime and :anychild tagged arguments that let the header, address and exists tests look at the headers of a part or of all of its children. It also adds three actions: replace, enclose and extracttext.
tldr.outcome: A filter can now route a message according to what is inside it, replace an unwanted part with text of its own, wrap the whole message in a warning, and copy the text of a part into a variable. Five capability strings, foreverypart, mime, replace, enclose and extracttext, tell a script what the server supports.

today: RFC 5703 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It registers the Sieve extensions foreverypart, mime, replace, enclose and extracttext, and the Original-Subject and Original-From message headers.

sections.title: What This Extension Adds
sections.content:
MIME messages are often complex objects, consisting of many parts and sub-parts. This Sieve extension defines mechanisms for performing tests on MIME body parts, looping through the MIME body parts, extracting information from a MIME body part, changing the contents of a MIME body part, and enclosing the entire message within a wrapper.

Five capability strings tell a script which of those mechanisms the server implements. A server that defines the foreverypart and break actions advertises foreverypart. A server that defines the :mime and :anychild tagged arguments to the header, address and exists commands advertises mime. A server that defines the replace action advertises replace, one that defines the enclose action advertises enclose, and one that defines the extracttext action advertises extracttext. To be useful, extracttext also requires the variables and foreverypart capabilities.

The IANA considerations register the five capability names in the registry of Sieve extensions, and register the Original-Subject and Original-From headers in the Permanent Message Header Fields registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension has five parts, and each has its own name that a script can ask about. A script that uses a name the server does not have is rejected at compile time rather than failing later.

sections.title: Looping Over the Parts of a Message
sections.content:
The base Sieve language has no looping mechanism. Given that messages may contain multiple parts, in order to support filters that apply to any and all parts, the extension introduces a new control command, foreverypart, which is an iterator that walks through every MIME part of a message, including nested parts, depth first, and applies the commands in the specified block to each of them. The iterator starts with the first MIME part as its current context and executes a command block, the Sieve commands enclosed by braces. On completion of the block, the iterator advances to the next MIME part and executes the same block again.

The iterator can be terminated prematurely by a new Sieve control command, break. The usage is foreverypart with an optional :name string followed by a block, and break with an optional :name string.

Foreverypart commands can be nested inside other foreverypart commands. When this occurs, the nested foreverypart iterates over the MIME parts contained within the MIME part currently being targeted by the nearest enclosing foreverypart command, so the inner loop only operates on children of the part currently accessed by the outer loop. If that MIME part is a terminal part, that is, it does not contain other MIME parts, the nested loop is simply ignored. Sieve implementations MAY limit the number of nested loops within one another, but they MUST support at least one nested loop inside another loop.

If a name is given to a break command, it terminates the closest enclosing loop with the identical matching name. If a nested foreverypart name is the same as a foreverypart name at an outer level, the outer level name is hidden. It is an error if there is no enclosing loop with that name. If no name is given in a break command, the break terminates the closest enclosing loop.
sections.plainLanguage:
The loop walks the message depth first: the top-level part, then each part inside it, then each part inside those. Inside the loop, the current part is what the tests and actions operate on.

Loops can be nested, and then the inner loop covers only the children of the part the outer loop is currently on. A named break stops one particular loop, which is how a script stops after the first matching part.

sections.title: The Extended header, address and exists Tests
sections.content:
The specification extends the base Sieve header, address and exists tests to support targeting those tests at a specific MIME part or at all MIME parts in the enclosing scope.

The header test gains the :mime and :anychild tagged arguments. The :anychild argument may only appear when the :mime argument is present, and presence of :anychild in the absence of :mime is an error. When used outside a foreverypart iterator without :anychild, the test examines only the outer top-level headers of the message. When used inside the iterator without :anychild, it examines the headers associated with the current MIME part context. When used outside the iterator with :anychild, it examines all MIME body parts and returns true if any of them satisfies the test. When used inside the iterator with :anychild, it examines the current part and all its nested body parts, again returning true if any satisfies the test.

With the :mime argument the header test can test individual elements of structured MIME headers. Implementations SHOULD support desegmentation, decoding and charset translation of parameter values encoded according to RFC 2231, and MAY decode RFC 2047-encoded words in parameter values. Four options are available. The :type option tests the MIME type of a Content-Type header, or the disposition of a Content-Disposition header, and uses a blank string for other headers. The :subtype option tests the MIME subtype of a Content-Type header and uses a blank string otherwise. The :contenttype option tests the combined type and subtype of a Content-Type header, behaves like :type for a Content-Disposition header, and uses a blank string otherwise. The :param option parses the header looking for MIME parameters and tests the named ones; the test returns true if any one named parameter value matches any of the test string values. When the :count option is used, the count is the number of headers that parsed successfully for :type, :subtype or :contenttype, and the number of parameters with the given name that were found for :param.

The address and exists tests gain the same two tagged arguments, and their behaviour with :anychild and the foreverypart iterator is the same as for the header test. Using either test with both arguments omitted is the test defined in RFC 5228, operating only on top-level header fields whether or not it is inside foreverypart. With :mime and no :anychild, it operates on the current MIME part only, or on the top-level header fields if outside foreverypart. With :mime and :anychild, it operates on the current MIME part and all of its descendants.
sections.plainLanguage: Three of the standard tests gain the ability to look inside a message. Without any new arguments they behave exactly as before, looking only at the top-level headers. With the mime argument they look at the headers of the current part, and with anychild as well they look at the headers of that part and of every part inside it.

sections.title: The replace Action
sections.content:
The replace command is defined to allow a MIME part to be replaced with the text supplied in the command. Its usage is replace with an optional :mime argument, an optional :subject string, an optional :from string, and a replacement string.

When used in the context of a foreverypart iterator, the MIME part to be replaced is the current MIME part. If the current MIME context is a multipart MIME part, the entire multipart part is replaced, which alters the MIME structure of the message by eliminating all of the children of the multipart part. Replacing a non-multipart part within a foreverypart loop context does not alter the overall message structure. If the MIME structure is altered, the change takes effect immediately: the foreverypart iterator that is executing does not go into the no-longer existing body parts, and subsequent foreverypart iterators would use the new message structure.

When used outside the context of a foreverypart loop, the MIME part to be replaced is the entire message. If the :mime parameter is not specified, the replacement string is a text/plain part in UTF-8. If it is specified, the replacement string is a MIME entity including both MIME headers and content.

If the entire message is being replaced, the optional :subject parameter specifies a subject line to attach to the generated message. UTF-8 characters can be used in the string, and implementations MUST convert the string to RFC 2047-encoded words if and only if non-ASCII characters are present. If the :subject parameter is used, implementations MUST preserve any previous Subject header as an Original-Subject header, and MUST preserve all other header fields from the original message with the exception of those relating to the MIME structure that is being replaced.

The optional :from parameter may be used to specify an alternate address for the From field of the generated message, as an indication that the message is no longer as created by the original author. The string must specify a valid RFC 5322 mailbox-list, and implementations SHOULD check the syntax and generate an error when a syntactically invalid parameter is specified. Implementations MAY also impose restrictions on what addresses can be specified, and it is suggested that values failing such a validity check simply be ignored rather than causing the replace action to fail. If the From header is changed, implementations MUST preserve the previous From header as an Original-From header. Implementations that support the editheader extension MUST ensure that any Original-Subject or Original-From headers added by the system cannot be modified or removed.

If :mime is specified and either :subject or :from is specified, the subject or from parameter MUST be ignored, and this SHOULD be flagged as a compilation error.
sections.plainLanguage:
Inside a loop, replace overwrites the part the loop is currently on with the given text. Outside a loop, it overwrites the whole message.

Replacing the whole message also replaces its headers, so the original subject and sender are kept under the names Original-Subject and Original-From. A script cannot then edit those two headers, because they record what the message originally was.

sections.title: The enclose Action
sections.content:
The enclose action allows an entire message to be enclosed as an attachment to a new message. After enclosure, subsequent actions affecting the message header or content, as well as tests operating on the MIME structure or accessing MIME header fields, use the newly created message instead of the original; this means that any use of a replace action or other similar actions should be executed before the enclose action.

If multiple enclose actions are executed by a script, the message is enclosed multiple times. A script that wants to choose between different enclosures, or wants to delay the enclosure to the end of the script, can use variables with appropriate tests.

The action does not affect messages that are forwarded via a redirect action.

Specifically, the original message becomes a multipart/mixed message with two parts: a text/plain portion with the string argument as its body, and a message/rfc822 portion with the original message enclosed. The Content-Type header field becomes multipart/mixed. The optional Subject header is specified by the :subject argument; if not present, the subject is taken from the enclosed message. Any headers specified by :headers are copied from the old message into the new message. If not specified by :headers, Date and From headers should be synthesized to reflect the current date and the user running the Sieve action.
sections.plainLanguage:
Enclose builds a new message around the old one. The new message has two parts: the text the script supplies, and the original message itself as an attachment.

Because the original is kept intact inside, the wrapping happens after any other edits, and a message that has been enclosed is the one later actions work on.

sections.title: The extracttext Action
sections.content:
The extracttext action may be used within the context of a foreverypart loop and is used to store text into a variable as defined by RFC 5229. Its usage is extracttext with an optional modifier, an optional :first number, and a variable name.

Servers MUST support transcoding of any textual body part into UTF-8 for use with this action. This requires decoding any transfer encoding as well as transcoding from the indicated character set into UTF-8. It stores at most the :first characters of the transcoded content of the current MIME body part in the variable identified by the variable name. If the :first parameter is not present, the whole content of the current MIME body part is stored. In either case the stored data MAY be truncated to conform to an implementation-specific limit on variable length and/or on MIME body part length. If the transfer encoding or character set is unrecognized by the implementation, or recognized but invalid, an empty string will result.

If extracttext is used outside the context of a foreverypart loop, the action sets the variable to the empty string, and this SHOULD be flagged as a compilation error. Modifiers are applied on the extracted text before it is stored in the variable.
sections.plainLanguage: This action copies the text of the current part into a variable, so that later parts of the script can compare against it or pass it on. The text is decoded and converted to UTF-8 first, so the script sees characters rather than encoded bytes.

sections.title: Example Scripts
sections.content:
The first example replaces some of the Windows executable attachments in a message. The script requires the foreverypart, mime and replace capabilities, walks every part, and replaces the part with a note if its content type is application/exe, or if a filename parameter in either the Content-Type or Content-Disposition header matches the pattern *.com.

The second example warns the user about executable attachment types instead of removing them. It requires the foreverypart, mime and enclose capabilities, walks every part, and when a filename parameter matches one of a list of patterns including *.com, *.exe, *.vbs, *.scr, *.pif, *.hta, *.bat and *.zip, it encloses the message with a warning text and then breaks out of the loop.

The third example extracts the subject and text out of messages from the boss. It requires the mime, variables and extracttext capabilities, checks whether the From header contains the boss's address, uses the :matches comparator to capture the value of the Subject header into a variable, and then loops over the parts to extract the first 100 characters of the first text part into another variable, breaking out of the loop once it has found one.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples cover the usual reasons to want this extension: removing an unwanted attachment, wrapping a message in a warning, and pulling a piece of text out of a message to use elsewhere.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The enclose action creates an entirely new message, as compared to just redirecting or forwarding the existing message. Any site policies applicable to message submission should therefore be enforced.

The looping specification provides easier access to information about the message contents, which may also be achieved through other Sieve tests. This is not believed to raise any additional security issues beyond those for the Sieve envelope and body tests.

Any change in message content may interfere with digital signature mechanisms that include that content in the signed material. In particular, using replace makes direct changes to the body content and will affect the body hash included in DKIM signatures, or the message signature used for S/MIME, Pretty Good Privacy or OpenPGP.

It is not possible to examine the MIME structure of decrypted content in a multipart/encrypted MIME part. When enclose is used on a message containing a multipart/signed MIME part, the Sieve implementation MUST ensure that the original message is copied octet-for-octet to maintain the validity of the digital signature.

The system MUST be sized and restricted in such a manner that even malicious use of MIME part matching does not deny service to other users of the host system. All of the security considerations given in the base Sieve specification also apply to these extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. A script that rewrites the body breaks any digital signature over the message, because the signature covers the original bytes. And a script that wraps a signed message must copy the original bytes exactly, so that the signature still verifies.
